c.tagline: Gateway to Angkor's ancient temple kingdoms.

taxi.fareNote: Tuk-tuks and taxis negotiate fixed fares upfront (no meters); typical in-town ride $2-4, day of temple touring by tuk-tuk $15-20

emergency.note: Tourist Police: 097 778 0002 / 012 402 424; response times can be slow outside central areas, private clinics (Royal Angkor International Hospital) recommended for serious issues

hood_landmark.Riverside/Old French Quarter: Preah Ang Chek Preah Ang Chorm Shrine, Siem Reap
hood_landmark.Svay Dangkum: Park Hyatt Siem Reap, Svay Dangkum

avoid.reason: Generally safe; touts around Angkor and tuk-tuk overcharging

hood_desc: The backpacker and nightlife hub around Pub Street and the Old Market, packed with restaurants, bars, massage shops and markets; best for first-timers who want everything walkable.
A leafy, laid-back riverside area a short walk/tuk-tuk from downtown with boutique guesthouses and good local restaurants; suits travelers wanting quiet nights but easy access to town.
A quieter residential-feeling area near the river north of downtown, popular with mid-range and boutique hotel guests seeking a calmer base still close to the action.
A rapidly developing strip southwest of downtown known for its concentration of budget hostels and value guesthouses; suits backpackers and budget travelers.
The upscale, garden-hotel enclave with Siem Reap's luxury resorts set among rice paddies northeast toward Angkor; suits honeymooners and travelers wanting a resort escape.

water.note: Not safe to drink from the tap; use bottled or filtered water, though commercial ice at tourist restaurants is usually fine.

transit.pay: Cash (USD or riel) paid directly to the driver; tuk-tuks and taxis are agreed by fixed fare before the ride, the small public bus network takes cash fares onboard. No rechargeable transit card system exists.
transit.hours: Tuk-tuks/taxis operate roughly 24 hours via hotels and apps; public buses run daytime hours only, roughly 5:30am-8pm
transit.note: There is no rail or metro system; nearly all visitor transport is by tuk-tuk, private car, or bicycle

train: Royal Railway Phnom Penh-Poipet line stops at Siem Reap (limited passenger service)
ferry: Seasonal boat to Tonle Sap floating villages/Phnom Penh via Tonle Sap Lake (dry-season dependent)

airport.name: Siem Reap–Angkor International Airport (SAI)
rentals: No major international rental counters on-site; cars typically hired with driver via hotels/agencies

tip.r: Not obligatory but appreciated; rounding up or 10% at restaurants and small tips for tuk-tuk/guide services are common

food.name: Fish amok
food.desc: Cambodia's signature dish: freshwater fish folded into a coconut-and-kroeung curry mousse, steamed soft in a banana-leaf cup or coconut shell.

places.name: Malis Siem Reap
places.note: Fine-Khmer garden restaurant; silky banana-leaf amok balanced with lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime.

places.name: Chanrey Tree
places.note: Refined Khmer cooking in a wooden house; amok served in a coconut shell, Kampot pepper on everything.

places.name: Khmer Kitchen Restaurant
places.note: Long-running budget favourite near Pub Street; amok around 5 USD, packed most nights.

food.name: Beef lok lak
food.desc: Cubes of beef seared in a peppery, soy-and-oyster glaze, piled on tomato and lettuce with rice, a fried egg and a Kampot pepper-lime dipping sauce.

places.name: Sugar Palm
places.note: Traditional wooden stilt house; classic lok lak and samlor korko taught to Gordon Ramsay here.

places.name: Madam Moch Khmer Restaurant
places.note: Family-run local kitchen praised for honest Khmer home cooking at local prices.

places.name: Khmer Kitchen Restaurant
places.note: Cheap, reliable lok lak with a proper black-pepper-and-lime dip; long queues at dinner.

food.name: Num banh chok
food.desc: The Khmer breakfast noodle: hand-pressed rice vermicelli under a green fish-and-lemongrass gravy, buried in raw banana flower, cucumber and herbs.

places.name: Phum Num Banh Chok
places.note: Riverside specialist with handmade noodles and ground river-fish gravy; relaxed garden setting.

places.name: Sam Khmer Noodles
places.note: Mornings only; curry-based broth over fresh vermicelli, a genuine local breakfast spot.

places.name: Psar Chas (Old Market) noodle ladies
places.note: Dawn stalls selling bowls for about 2 USD; the way locals actually eat it.

food.name: Bai sach chrouk
food.desc: Breakfast of thin pork slices grilled over coals after a coconut-and-garlic marinade, served over broken rice with pickles and a bowl of clear broth.

places.name: Wat Bo Street morning stalls
places.note: Charcoal grills fire up around 6am; the smell finds you before the stall does.

places.name: Psar Leu Market food row
places.note: Big local market well away from tourists; cheapest and most authentic version in town.

places.name: Sister Srey Cafe
places.note: Social-enterprise cafe doing a tidy sit-down version for visitors wary of street stalls.

food.name: Samlor korko
food.desc: The everyday Khmer stirring soup: a dozen vegetables, toasted ground rice and prahok simmered with fish or pork into something earthy and slightly bitter.

places.name: Sugar Palm
places.note: One of the few tourist-facing kitchens that cooks korko the traditional, unsweetened way.

places.name: Malis Siem Reap
places.note: Polished version of the country soup with heritage vegetables; good introduction to Khmer bitterness.

places.name: Mie Cafe
places.note: Chef-owned Khmer kitchen with a rotating seasonal take on korko and other village soups.

food.name: Prahok ktis
food.desc: Minced pork simmered with coconut cream and prahok fermented fish paste into a pungent dip, scooped up with raw cucumber, cabbage and long beans.

places.name: Marum
places.note: Training restaurant in a candlelit garden; Khmer classics as shareable plates, red-ant stir-fry too.

places.name: Sugar Palm
places.note: Full-strength prahok ktis with a proper platter of raw vegetables, not toned down for tourists.

places.name: Madam Moch Khmer Restaurant
places.note: Home-style kitchen where the prahok is used the way Cambodian families use it.

food.name: Sombai rice-wine liqueur
food.desc: Cambodian rice spirit infused with local spices, herbs and fruit - anise, ginger-red chilli, mango-green tea - and sold in hand-painted bottles.

places.name: Sombai Cambodian Liqueur
places.note: Tasting room and infusion workshop in a timber house; sample the full flavour range before buying.

places.name: Miss Wong Cocktail Bar
places.note: 1920s Shanghai-style bar mixing Khmer liqueurs and kaffir-lime cocktails; a Siem Reap institution.

places.name: Asana Old Wooden House
places.note: Last traditional wooden house in town; rice-wine cocktails served on floor cushions.

food.name: Tuk ompov (sugarcane juice)
food.desc: Cane pressed through a hand-cranked mangle with a wedge of kaffir lime, poured over ice - the standard antidote to an afternoon at Angkor.

places.name: Psar Chas (Old Market) juice carts
places.note: Half a dozen presses working all day; ask for extra lime to cut the sweetness.

places.name: Angkor Night Market stalls
places.note: Evening carts pressing cane to order, usually under 1 USD a glass.

places.name: Psar Leu Market
places.note: Local market prices and the freshest cane; also good for palm-sugar drinks.

landmarks: Angkor Wat
The largest religious monument on Earth, this 12th-century Khmer temple's five lotus towers and reflecting moat make it Cambodia's most photographed sunrise silhouette.
Bayon Temple
Angkor Thom's central temple is famous for its 200-plus enigmatic stone faces smiling serenely from towering spires, a hypnotic maze for photographers.
Ta Prohm
Made famous by Tomb Raider, this jungle temple is dramatically entwined by massive silk-cotton and strangler fig tree roots swallowing its ancient stone walls.
Angkor Thom
The last great Khmer capital's fortified walls and iconic South Gate, lined with rows of stone giants holding a writhing naga serpent, awe every visitor.
Banteay Srei
Nicknamed the 'Citadel of Women,' this small pink sandstone temple dazzles with the most intricate, deeply carved decorative reliefs in all of Angkor.
Phnom Bakheng
Perched atop a forested hill, this pyramid temple is Siem Reap's premier sunset viewpoint, offering sweeping panoramas over the jungle toward Angkor Wat.
Tonlé Sap Lake
Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake is home to stilted and floating fishing villages, offering boat tours through a vibrant, water-based way of life.
Angkor National Museum
A modern showcase of over a thousand Khmer artifacts and statues, this museum offers essential context and dazzling close-up detail before touring the temples themselves.
Wat Preah Prom Rath
This working Buddhist temple in central Siem Reap charms visitors with golden stupas, colorful murals, and whimsical statues of oxen and horses out front.
Pub Street
The neon-lit heart of Siem Reap's nightlife, this pedestrian strip buzzes with street food stalls, bars, and market vendors, capturing the city's energetic modern side.

train.note: No railway serves Siem Reap. Cambodia's Royal Railway network runs only from Phnom Penh (to Poipet on the Thai border and to Sihanoukville), bypassing Siem Reap entirely - use buses instead.

bus.note: Direct international coaches to Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City depart Siem Reap daily; Giant Ibis lets you book online. Passengers clear immigration at the Poipet (Thailand) or Bavet (Vietnam) border. Carry passport and any required visa.

ferry.note: No international ferries. A scenic domestic boat crosses Tonle Sap lake to Battambang (and formerly Phnom Penh), but it runs only in the wet season when water levels are high - confirm locally before booking.

half.name: Battambang
half.blurb: Riverside Cambodian city known for French colonial architecture and rural charm.

full.name: Phnom Penh
full.blurb: Cambodia's riverside capital known for palaces, temples, and a poignant history.

full.name: Nakhon Ratchasima
full.blurb: Gateway city to Thailand's Isaan region, known as Korat, rich in ancient Khmer ruins.

full.name: Ubon Ratchathani
full.blurb: Northeastern Thai city known for its candle festival and riverside temples.

full.name: Surin
full.blurb: Northeastern Thai city famed for its annual elephant round-up festival and Khmer heritage.

full.name: Warin Chamrap
full.blurb: Thai town in Isan known for its local markets and rural surroundings.
